title: Dominic and the Radiators
premise: Ada Crane has spent two decades as a night librarian in a city that never quite sleeps, keeping her voice low and her grief lower—she never told her dying mother she loved her, and she never told anyone that the song 'Radiators' was written by her brother Dominic, who died before he could record it. When she hears his unwritten song playing on a late-night radio program, credited to a stranger, Ada is pulled out of her carefully maintained invisibility into a quiet war over authorship, memory, and justice that no court will hear. As she traces how the song escaped into the world, she must finally speak the words she withheld from her mother, at her grave, before Alzheimer's erases even the memory of what was left unsaid. The novel ends not with vindication but with release: Ada records the song herself, badly, on an old cassette, and mails it to no one.
about_author: Rosalind Blackwood is the pen name of a former night-shift archivist who spent eleven years cataloguing unclaimed recordings in a municipal library. She writes about grief, cities, and the small illegalities of love, and lives near a radiator she refuses to fix.

chapters.title: The Hours Between Two and Four
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. We meet Ada shelving books in the dead hours of the Meridian Public Library, a woman who has perfected the art of almost saying things. Her routines are rituals of avoidance: unanswered letters, a brother's name never spoken. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as competence.

chapters.title: A Song That Was Never Recorded
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Driving home at dawn, the radio plays a song called 'Radiators'—Dominic's song, note for note, though he died before ever recording it. Ada pulls over, shaking. Emotional beat: the past breaking through the present like water through a ceiling.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Ada's POV. The story of Dominic: the basement piano, the song he wrote for their mother, his death at nineteen, and the funeral where Ada couldn't speak. Then their mother's decline, and the phone call Ada let ring. Emotional beat: guilt calcifying into identity.

chapters.title: The Voice on the Radio
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She tracks the broadcast to a late-night program hosted by a man named Ellis Vann, who credits the song to a singer-songwriter called Marty Fell. Ada writes a letter, then burns it; then writes another and keeps it. Emotional beat: the first crack in her invisibility.

chapters.title: Marty Fell
chapters.summary: Marty's POV, first appearance. A fading musician in his fifties who genuinely believes 'Radiators' is his own—he heard it once, decades ago, in a dream he thinks. His career is dying and this song is his last chance. Emotional beat: sympathetic delusion, the tragedy of stolen memory.

chapters.title: What the Archive Keeps
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Searching the library's uncatalogued holdings, Ada finds a cassette labeled in Dominic's handwriting—a home recording she didn't know existed, donated years ago in a box of unclaimed property. Proof, and a wound reopened. Emotional beat: hope arriving as grief.

chapters.title: Ellis Vann, Night Shift
chapters.summary: Ellis's POV. The radio host remembers receiving the tape anonymously years ago and passing it along; he owes someone a favor and doesn't ask questions. Ada visits the station, and for the first time says her brother's name aloud to a stranger. Emotional beat: testimony beginning.

chapters.title: The Mother's Memory Goes Entirely
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada visits her mother, Ines, now in a care facility, whose dementia has nearly erased Dominic altogether. Ines hums 'Radiators' without knowing why. Ada almost tells her everything, and again doesn't. Emotional beat: the cost of silence compounding daily.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Ada consults a weary intellectual-property lawyer, Dana Okafor, who explains the brutal truth: no registration, no estate, no case. What Ada wants isn't damages anyway—it's acknowledgment, which no court can order. Emotional beat: the law's limits clarifying what she actually needs.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Half-Light Club
chapters.summary: Alternating Ada/Marty POV. Ada attends Marty's performance of 'Radiators' and waits for him afterward. She tells him the truth; he calls her a liar, then a thief, then—when she plays Dominic's cassette—goes silent. Emotional beat: collision, and the strange intimacy of shared possession.

chapters.title: The Dream Defense
chapters.summary: Marty's POV. Marty interrogates his own past: a hostel in 1989, a boy playing piano through a wall, a melody absorbed so deeply it became his. He begins to suspect his entire career is built on other people's ghosts. Emotional beat: vertigo of self-erasure.

chapters.title: Letters to No One
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada finds the unsent letters she's written for twenty years—to Dominic, to her mother—and reads them all in one night. Interwoven: fragments of the letters themselves. Emotional beat: inventory of silence, and its terrible weight.

chapters.title: Dana's Bargain
chapters.summary: Dana's POV. Okafor proposes an off-law solution: public attribution through the radio station, a documented provenance, Marty's voluntary co-credit. It requires both Ada and Marty to agree to be vulnerable in public. Emotional beat: justice as negotiation rather than verdict.

chapters.title: Marty Comes to the Library
chapters.summary: Ada and Marty POV alternating. Marty appears at the night desk, humbled, asking to hear the cassette again. They listen together in the empty reading room. He asks who wrote it; she says, 'My brother. His name was Dominic.' Emotional beat: witness, at last.

chapters.title: Ines, Briefly Clear
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. A rare lucid moment: Ines recognizes Ada and asks about 'the boy and his song.' Ada starts to answer honestly—and Ines slips away mid-sentence, the window closing. Emotional beat: urgency sharpened into desperation; time is running out.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Ellis's POV. Ellis agrees to air a segment: the original cassette, the story of Dominic Crane, Marty's confession of borrowed memory. Ada listens from the stacks as her brother's name travels across the sleepless city. Emotional beat: terror and exaltation of being seen.

chapters.title: Backlash
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Not everyone applauds: Marty's old fans call Ada a fraud chasing royalties; a music blog dissects the story cruelly; the library board questions her judgment. Ada wavers, tempted to retreat into invisibility. Emotional beat: the price of speaking, and the temptation to recant.

chapters.title: What Marty Owes
chapters.summary: Marty's POV. Marty, ruined and relieved, plays his final show and introduces 'Radiators' with Dominic's name and the true story. He gives Ada the only thing she asked for: the sentence, said publicly, plainly. Emotional beat: restitution without redemption, and peace in that.

chapters.title: Saying Goodbye Properly
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. At Ines's bedside, in her final days, Ada says everything—the apology, the love, the whole twenty years—at last, out loud, whether or not her mother can hear. Ines hums the song one more time. Emotional beat: catharsis; the central debt paid.

chapters.title: After the Funeral of Words
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. After Ines dies, Ada sorts the estate and finds her mother kept every clipping about Dominic—including a review of the radio broadcast, saved in her lucid months. Her mother knew. Emotional beat: grief transfigured; the discovery that silence was never total.

chapters.title: Recording
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. In the library after hours, with Ellis's borrowed recorder, Ada sings 'Radiators'—badly, off-key, crying halfway through—and keeps going. It is not a performance; it is a burial and a birth. Emotional beat: claiming voice, imperfectly, finally.

chapters.title: The Radiator Hums
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, coda. Months later: the cassette mailed to no one, the song drifting back onto the radio with the right name attached, Ada still working nights but no longer hiding. The radiator in her apartment hums its old note, and she hums back. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; memory carried forward, spoken at last.
